analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicare coverage of home nursing and aide services, paid for by a higher payroll tax cap.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past subcommittee referral in the House and received no cosponsors and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would loosen Medicare's definition of "intermittent" home health care, so patients needing daily nursing or aide visits at home — including short stretches of seven-day care — could keep getting Medicare coverage instead of losing it or entering a facility. To pay for it, the bill would raise the ceiling on wages subject to the Medicare hospital insurance payroll tax, spreading the cost toward higher earners. It was referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, where it stalled.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who need substantial home nursing or home health aide services — for example, patients recovering from illness who need care every day for weeks. Under then-current rules, care that rose to a daily level could fall outside Medicare's home health benefit; this bill would keep that care covered, letting people receive skilled care at home rather than in a hospital or nursing facility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare patients needing daily home care

how_it_helps.text: Defines nursing and home health aide services as "intermittent" when needed fewer than 7 days a week, or up to 40 consecutive days when needed daily, so more at-home care stays within Medicare's covered benefit.
Applies the expanded coverage to home health periods beginning on or after January 1, 1994.

Pays for the expansion by raising the wage ceiling for the Medicare hospital insurance payroll tax, adding $5,000 to the 1993 base in 1994 and indexing the cap thereafter, which shifts more of the cost onto higher-wage earners.

analysis.who_pays: Higher-wage workers and their employers, who would owe Medicare payroll taxes on a larger share of wages. The hospital insurance tax is paid half by the worker and half by the employer, so some of the cost could show up as lower wage growth. General beneficiaries would face no new premium under the bill text.

drawbacks.text: The financing is a payroll tax increase, and payroll taxes fall on wages rather than investment income, so even a higher cap leaves substantial earnings above the ceiling untaxed; critics of payroll-tax financing generally note this limits how progressive the funding can be.

Expanding the home health benefit would add federal Medicare spending, and broader home health coverage creates revenue for home care agencies, which raises the familiar concern that a more generous benefit invites greater use and cost growth over time.
The bill arrived with no cosponsors [S4] and no committee action beyond referral, so it never received a hearing, amendment process, or floor debate where its design could be tested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a specific group of Medicare patients: keeping skilled daily care at home covered is usually cheaper and better for patients than a nursing facility stay, and home care is typically less expensive than institutional care. The cost is a real but moderate payroll tax increase aimed above the middle of the wage scale. The bigger problem was process, not design: the bill was never debated, so its financing details were never examined or improved. It was a narrow, single-sponsor bill with no visible coalition behind it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, sent to their health subcommittees days later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Hoagland introduced the bill on January 5, 1993, the first day of the 103rd Congress.
The House referred it jointly to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
On January 8, 1993, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; on February 24, 1993, it was also referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health.
No further action is recorded, and the bill lists zero cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one acted on the bill, so the financing arrangement under current law remained in place: higher-wage earners paid no added Medicare payroll tax, and home health agencies gained no new covered revenue. Medicare patients needing extended daily home care received no new coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Higher earners and the status quo

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 103rd Congress and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Health and took no further recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Health and the Environment and took no further recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and it never reached a vote, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Home health agencies and home care providers
industries.note: A broader "intermittent" definition would let more patients qualify for Medicare-covered home nursing and aide services, sending more reimbursed work to home care agencies. Patients gain coverage at the same time, and home care typically costs Medicare less than facility care, so the industry's gain runs alongside the beneficiary's gain here.

Broader home health coverage could shift some care out of nursing facilities and hospitals, reducing admissions that those facilities are paid for. Patients generally prefer and benefit from care at home.

The bill would raise the wage ceiling on the Medicare hospital insurance payroll tax, so workers with wages above the old cap would owe more payroll tax, along with their employers. Their financial interest ran against the expansion's beneficiaries.
